The Vision

We are building a world model for financial markets — a system that understands the economy the way a chess engine understands chess. Not by memorising past games, but by understanding the rules, the pieces, and the consequences of every move.

Every major AI system that has changed the world — AlphaGo, self-driving cars, protein folding — works the same way: it builds an internal model of how the world works, then uses that model to reason, plan, and act. Finance has nothing like this. The biggest banks in the world spend $40 billion a year on technology and still rely on dashboards that show what already happened. They have faster data. They do not have better understanding.

RecWM is the missing piece: an AI system that doesn’t just predict prices, but understands why markets move, how decisions create consequences, and what happens when everyone acts on the same information at the same time.

In one sentence: RecWM is an on-premise AI engine that models the causal structure of financial markets, learns continuously from new data without forgetting the past, and accounts for the fact that its own predictions change the system it’s predicting.

The Problem: Why This Doesn’t Exist Yet

To understand why nobody has built this, you need to understand three things that make financial markets fundamentally harder than other AI problems:

Problem 1: The World Changes

A chess board has fixed rules. A protein has fixed physics. Financial markets do not. The relationship between interest rates and stock prices behaves completely differently in 2007 (before the financial crisis), 2010 (zero interest rates), and 2022 (fastest rate hikes in 40 years). A model trained on one regime breaks the moment conditions change.

This is called non-stationarity, and it kills every model that trains once and deploys with frozen weights. Which is every model deployed at major banks today.

Problem 2: The Model Changes the World

This is the hard one. When a weather forecast predicts rain, the rain still comes. When a financial model predicts a crash and people act on it, the prediction itself changes whether the crash happens. If everyone hedges, the crash might be averted. If everyone sells, the crash gets worse.

George Soros called this reflexivity. Academics call it performativity. It means that in financial markets, the observer is not separate from the system — the model is inside the world it’s trying to model. This creates a feedback loop that standard AI completely ignores.

Why this matters practically: Every risk model at every major bank ignores this. They assume the model observes the market from outside. But when JPMorgan’s risk model and Goldman’s risk model and everyone else’s risk model all see the same signal and all act on it simultaneously — that collective action is the event. The models didn’t predict the crash. They caused it. And they have no mechanism to know this is happening.

Problem 3: Constraints Are Invisible

Markets don’t just have prices. They have rules. Regulations cap leverage. Liquidity determines what trades are actually possible. Accounting identities mean that one party’s asset is another’s liability. These constraints are not bolted on after the fact — they shape what can happen before anyone acts. And they change over time: a new regulation, a liquidity drought, a collateral haircut change all alter the space of possible outcomes.

No existing model treats constraints as first-class objects that evolve with the system.

The three-problem summary

ProblemWhat It MeansWhat Everyone Else DoesWhat RecWM Does

The Core Insight: Markets Build Themselves

Here is the idea that makes RecWM different from everything else:

Financial markets are not systems to be predicted. They are systems that are continuously constructed by the beliefs and actions of their participants, under constraints that themselves evolve.

Think about it this way. When you see a stock price, you’re not seeing a measurement of some external reality (like a thermometer measuring temperature). You’re seeing the result of thousands of people acting on their beliefs about what the stock is worth. Their beliefs drive their actions. Their actions change the price. The new price changes their beliefs. And around it goes.

This is the reflexive loop at the heart of all financial markets:

Beliefs → Actions → World Changes → Beliefs Update → …

This loop is not a bug to be linearised away. It is the fundamental mechanism of financial markets.

RecWM’s core equation captures this in four pieces:

W(t+1) = C( W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t) )

In plain English:

  • W(t) — the world state right now (prices, order books, macro data, narratives)
  • B(t) — what everyone believes about the world right now
  • A(B) — the actions those beliefs produce (trades, speeches, regulations)
  • Φ(t) — the constraints that filter what’s possible (regulations, liquidity, physics)
  • C(·) — the construction operator that combines actions + constraints to produce the next world state

Every other model asks: “Given the past, what happens next?” RecWM asks: “What can be constructed, by whom, under what constraints, and how will the act of construction change future possibilities?”

What the Model Is

RecWM is a structured intelligence engine that runs entirely on the client’s own hardware. Let’s be precise about what it is and what it is not:

What it IS

  • A causal model of how financial markets work
  • Continuously learning — gets smarter every day
  • On-premise — your data never leaves your building
  • Traceable — every output links back to the data and logic that produced it
  • Reflexivity-aware — knows when its own predictions are affecting the market
  • Constraint-native — regulations and limits are baked in, not bolted on

What it is NOT

  • Not a chatbot sitting on a price feed
  • Not a dashboard that shows what already happened
  • Not a black box — every number is explainable
  • Not a prediction machine that says “the market will go up”
  • Not a 50-billion-parameter language model — it’s much smaller and more structured
  • Not a cloud service — it runs on your own GPUs

High-Level Architecture

Before diving into the details, here is the full picture of how RecWM works — from raw data to actionable intelligence — in a single view. Every box below is explained in the sections that follow.

Reading the Diagram

The architecture flows top to bottom through seven layers. Understanding each layer and why it exists is the key to understanding RecWM:

Layer 1: Data Ingestion

All data comes from free, institutional-grade sources — FRED for macro and rates, Yahoo Finance for prices, SEC EDGAR for corporate filings, GDELT for real-time events, central bank feeds for policy signals, and funding market data for liquidity stress. Client proprietary data can be plugged in as an additional feed. The raw data is the same data available to everyone; the edge is entirely in how it gets processed.

Layer 2: Typed Fragment Decomposition

The raw data is decomposed into seven typed fragments, each capturing a different aspect of financial reality at its natural timescale. The green bars show update frequency — Liquidity and Sentiment update almost continuously; Structure and Policy sit frozen most of the time, opening only for genuine structural breaks. This decomposition is not arbitrary — it is derived from the mathematical structure of how financial systems actually evolve (Theorem 4).

Layer 3: Per-Fragment Processing

Each fragment passes through three stages: SPIB compression strips away noise and keeps only information that predicts the future (fast fragments get heavy compression, slow fragments get gentle treatment). GateL0RD gating decides when each fragment should update its state — closed gates preserve memory perfectly. S5 state-space models run each fragment at its own clock speed via typed discretisation steps.

Layer 4: Composition + Constraints

The composition operator ⊗ combines all seven fragments into a single world state, respecting the causal relationships between them (e.g., liquidity → risk → credit). Simultaneously, the constraint filter Φ(t) removes any state that violates regulatory limits, liquidity floors, physical settlement rules, or accounting identities. Constraints are not checked after the fact — they shape the space of possible outcomes before anything is predicted.

Layer 5: Reflexivity Engine

This is what makes RecWM unique. The reflexivity engine measures the feedback loop: Beliefs → Actions → World Changes → Beliefs Update. The reflexivity coefficient ε(t) quantifies how much the model’s own predictions are influencing reality. Near 0 means safe observation; above 0.3 means danger — self-fulfilling dynamics are forming. The dashed line looping back is the fundamental mechanism of financial markets that every other model ignores.

Layer 6: Monte Carlo Forward Simulation

Starting from the current composed world state, the model runs 256–1,024 forward simulations sampling from its uncertainty about each fragment. Simulations that violate constraints are removed, not adjusted. What survives is a distribution of futures that are actually possible — not point predictions, but probability-weighted scenarios grounded in causal structure.

Layer 7: Derived Intelligence

Four proprietary signals emerge from the simulated futures. These are not technical indicators derived from price charts — they emerge from the structure of the world model itself. Each signal measures a different aspect of systemic health: how much of the economy is feasible (Constructibility), how self-referential the market is (Reflexive Instability), whether stable parts create an unstable whole (Composition Fragility), and whether today’s decisions lock in irreversible trajectories (Path Lock-In).

The Cyan Sidebar: Continual Learning

Running alongside the entire pipeline is the continual learning stack — five layered mechanisms that keep the model current without forgetting the past. Gate-based memory preserves old knowledge; streaming updates incorporate new data in real time; EWC protects critical parameters; BOCPD detects regime changes; and a slow-fast blend anchors rapid adaptation to a stable foundation. The model gets smarter every day without retraining from scratch.

What Goes In: The Data

RecWM ingests the entire observable financial world. All from free, institutional-grade data sources — no Bloomberg terminal required.

Credit & Liquidity

GDP, CPI, unemployment, payrolls, PMI, trade data, IMF forecasts, World Bank structural indicators, debt-to-GDP ratios

News & Sentiment

GDELT global event database (every 15 minutes), geopolitical event detection, news tone analysis, narrative regime identification

Corporate Filings

SEC EDGAR: 10-K/10-Q financial statements (XBRL structured data), 8-K event filings, insider transactions, leverage ratios

The key insight: the raw data is free. FRED, BIS, EDGAR, Yahoo Finance — anyone can access it. The edge is not in the data. The edge is in how the data is structured: decomposed into seven typed fragments, each operating at its natural timescale, and processed through a model that understands causal relationships instead of just correlations.

How It Works: The Engine

The model works in seven stages. Think of it as an assembly line: raw data enters at the bottom, and actionable intelligence comes out at the top.

Stage 1: Break the World into Pieces

The first thing the model does is break the financial world into seven fragments, each capturing a different aspect of reality at its natural speed:

FragmentWhat It CapturesSpeedExample
LiquidityCan you actually trade?Hours to daysBid-ask spreads widening, funding markets freezing
MomentumWhich way are things moving?Days to weeksTech stocks rallying, EM currencies selling off
RiskHow much uncertainty is there?Weeks to monthsVIX spiking, correlations rising, tail risks growing
CreditWho can pay their debts?Months to quartersCredit spreads widening, leverage building up
StructureWhat are the deep trends?Quarters to yearsDemographic shifts, secular stagnation, de-globalisation
SentimentWhat’s the narrative?Hours to days“Soft landing” narrative, geopolitical fear, AI hype
PolicyWhat are governments doing?MonthsFed pivoting dovish, ECB holding, fiscal stimulus

Why this matters: A volatility spike means completely different things at different timescales. At the 5-day scale, it’s a liquidity event. At the 60-day scale, it’s a regime shift. At the 250-day scale, it’s a structural break. The model doesn’t predict “the market” — it predicts each fragment at its natural timescale and composes the results.

Stage 2: Learn What Matters (Compress)

Each fragment has a huge amount of raw data. The model compresses each fragment down to only the information that helps predict the future. Fast, noisy fragments (like tick-by-tick price data) get compressed aggressively — most of the noise is market microstructure, not signal. Slow fragments (like policy signals) get compressed gently — every rare policy signal is valuable and must be preserved.

Stage 3: Decide When to Update (Gate)

Not every fragment needs to update at every moment. The model learns when each fragment should change its state. In practice:

  • Liquidity and Momentum update almost continuously — markets move fast
  • Structure and Policy stay frozen 95%+ of the time, then spike open for a few steps when there’s a genuine data release or regime break

When a gate is closed, the fragment’s state is preserved exactly as it was — no forgetting, no drift. This is the model’s built-in memory: it naturally remembers what it learned about slow-moving dynamics while quickly adapting to fast-moving ones.

Stage 4: Compose the Fragments

The fragments don’t exist in isolation. Liquidity affects risk. Credit affects structure. Policy affects everything. The model learns how fragments interact — not just correlations, but causal relationships (if liquidity dries up, then risk spikes, because market makers withdraw).

At this stage, constraints kick in. Four types of constraints filter every possible action:

  • Regulatory — leverage caps, position limits, capital requirements
  • Liquidity — you can’t sell what nobody will buy
  • Physical — commodity delivery, settlement cycles, infrastructure limits
  • Accounting — one party’s asset is another’s liability; balance sheets must balance

Stage 5: Measure Reflexivity

This is where RecWM does something no other model does. It asks: “If I publish this prediction and people act on it, how much will the world change as a result?”

The answer is a single number: the reflexivity coefficient ε(t). Think of it as a dial:

  • ε near 0: Normal markets. Predictions are reliable. The model is observing, not influencing.
  • ε around 0.3: Danger zone. Feedback loops are forming. Confidence intervals should be widened. Point estimates are becoming unreliable.
  • ε above 0.4: Crisis dynamics. Selling begets selling. The model’s predictions are becoming self-fulfilling. This is 2008, COVID, the UK gilt crisis territory.

Stage 6: Simulate the Future

Starting from the current state of all seven fragments, the model runs 256–1,024 forward simulations. Each simulation samples from the model’s uncertainty about each fragment, producing a distribution of possible futures — not a single prediction. Simulations that violate constraints (regulatory limits, liquidity floors) are removed, not patched. The surviving simulations represent the set of futures that are actually possible.

Stage 7: Produce Intelligence

From the simulated futures, four proprietary signals emerge. These are not technical indicators derived from price — they emerge from the structure of the world model itself:

Constructibility Index

What fraction of possible actions are currently feasible? When this drops, the economy is becoming rigid — fewer things are possible, fewer trades can execute, fewer policies can work. Leads traditional financial conditions indices by 1–4 weeks.

Reflexive Instability

How much are predictions influencing reality? When this is high, self-fulfilling prophecy conditions exist. The market is not just being observed — it’s being shaped by the models observing it. Values above 0.3 are dangerous.

Composition Fragility

Can stable parts create an unstable whole? Two individually safe positions can become dangerous when combined. This is the mathematical definition of systemic risk — risk that exists only in the interaction, not in the components.

Path Lock-In

How sensitive is the future to decisions made today? When this approaches 1, you’re at a fork in the road — small choices now lock in trajectories that cannot be reversed later. Bifurcation points, tipping points, points of no return.

What Comes Out

Every output from RecWM has three properties: it is quantified (numbers with confidence intervals, not vague assessments), traceable (every number links back to the specific data, fragments, and logic that produced it), and actionable (it tells you what to do, not just what happened).

Example: Regime Change Alert

The model continuously monitors all seven fragments for structural breaks. When it detects a regime shift, it produces an alert like this:

[REGIME SHIFT ALERT]
Transition: “Late-cycle credit expansion” → “Liquidity contraction”
Confidence: 68%

What triggered it:
  • Funding costs jumped (USD basis widened 18bps in 3 days)
  • Correlations spiked (0.31 → 0.58 across asset classes)
  • Reflexivity rising (ε: 0.12 → 0.34 — selling is feeding on itself)

This looks like: August 2015 (81% similar), Feb 2018 VIX (74% similar)
But different because: credit-to-GDP gap is 12pp wider than 2015,
  and the Fed is cutting (not holding). This changes the recovery path.

Full trace: [view data sources] [view causal graph]

Notice what’s different from a Bloomberg alert: it tells you why the regime is shifting (not just that it happened), it identifies the structural analog (not just a similar price pattern), and it tells you where today diverges from the analog. The divergence is often the most valuable part.

Example: Scenario Analysis

A portfolio manager asks: “What happens if the Fed cuts 50bps and China devalues by 3%?”

The model runs both interventions simultaneously through all seven fragments, capturing interaction effects (a Fed cut combined with China devaluation compounds EM outflow pressure beyond either shock alone). After 5,000 forward simulations:

Scenario: Fed −50bps + China devalues 3%
20-day horizon • 5,000 simulations • 4,847 survived constraints

S&P 500       +1.8%   (range: −6.1% to +9.4%)
US Dollar     −2.1%   (range: −4.8% to +0.3%)
EM Currencies −4.7%   (range: −11.2% to −0.9%)
Gold          +3.2%   (range: −0.5% to +7.8%)
HY Spreads    +38bp   (range: +8bp to +95bp)

Main story: In 58% of simulations, equities rally initially
on the rate cut, then reverse within 8 days as EM outflows
overwhelm the tailwind.

Reflexivity warning: ε=0.34 — the initial market reaction
will itself alter the Fed’s next move. This is path-dependent.

The model doesn’t just give you a point estimate. It gives you a distribution of outcomes, the dominant transmission path (which causal chain is most likely), and a reflexivity warning (will acting on this information change the outcome?).

The Hedge Fund Playbook: How You Make Money With This

RecWM is not an analytics dashboard. It is an alpha generation engine. Every capability maps directly to P&L. Here is how hedge funds — from discretionary macro to multi-strategy platforms — use it to generate alpha, deploy capital, manage risk, and avoid the blowups that destroy firms.

The core claim: Regime-conditional models add 100–200bps annualised and 0.15–0.3 Sharpe improvement over static models (Ang & Bekaert, Review of Financial Studies, 2002; Guidolin & Timmermann, JEDC, 2007). Nearly all of this alpha comes from early transition detection — being underweight risk 2–4 weeks before a regime flips captures the bulk of the drawdown-avoidance benefit. Late detection captures almost none. RecWM is built to detect transitions early.

1. Thesis Generation — Finding the Next Big Trade

The hardest part of running money is generating a thesis that is both non-consensus and correct. Bridgewater decomposes markets into growth and inflation surprises versus what’s discounted, using 100 years of cross-country data to match structural analogs (Weimar, 1930s deleveraging, Japan 1990s) — Dalio’s Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises formalises this as template-matching. Soros built theses around reflexive feedback loops (1992 ERM short: rate/currency-peg incompatibility). Brevan Howard runs off central bank reaction functions, cross-currency basis, and positioning data.

The common bottleneck: analysts manually pattern-match today’s data against a mental library of past regimes, and cross-fragment causality (how a Liquidity shock propagates through Credit into Structure) is inferred qualitatively. RecWM automates this — turning Dalio-style analog-matching into a queryable, continuously-updated, backtestable causal model.

Macro Thesis Discovery

The model continuously tracks all 7 fragments and their causal connections. When the causal graph shifts — a relationship that held for years starts breaking — it surfaces a thesis candidate with the structural analog, divergence analysis, and confidence interval.

Example: “The credit-to-liquidity transmission channel has inverted for the first time since 2007. Credit stress is no longer causing liquidity withdrawal — instead, liquidity withdrawal is causing credit stress. This inversion preceded the GFC by 14 months. Current analog similarity: 72%. Key divergence: EM external debt is 2.4× higher, concentrating risk in 3 countries.”

Cross-Asset Dislocation Finder

When the causal graph implies one price and the market shows another, that gap is a trade. The model quantifies the dislocation, identifies the mechanism that should close it, and estimates the timeline. This covers credit-equity basis (CDS-implied vol vs. equity IV), rates-FX (covered interest parity deviations), and vol-rates (swaption vol vs. realised rate vol).

Why causal beats statistical: Standard RV uses cointegration and regression — these assume stationary linear relationships and break when regimes shift (2020 COVID, 2022 UK gilt crisis), producing worst drawdowns precisely when the trade should be sized up. RecWM conditions the relationship on regime state. Credit-equity correlation is near 0 in calm markets, spikes to 0.6–0.8 in stress — a causal model sizes the trade for which regime is forming, not a rolling-window average.

Narrative Decay Detection

Markets run on narratives (“soft landing,” “AI revolution,” “higher for longer”). Sentiment alone is coincident or lagging. RecWM detects narrative decay — the cross-fragment divergence where Sentiment is still bullish but Structure is deteriorating (decreasing breadth, rising crowding, thinning liquidity). This divergence historically precedes reversals by 1–3 weeks.

Example: “The ‘soft landing’ narrative has positive sentiment momentum but manufacturing PMI contracted for 3 consecutive months. In 6/7 prior instances, this Sentiment-Structure divergence resolved via narrative collapse and a 6–12% equity drawdown within 40 trading days.”

Regime-Transition Thesis

The biggest trades come from regime changes. RecWM detects these early, identifies the structural analog, and tells you where this episode diverges from the analog — the divergence is often the most valuable information, because it tells you what the consensus is getting wrong.

Alpha: Global macro funds run Sharpe ~0.5–0.8 with 8–15% vol. Regime-conditional overlays add 100–200bps annualised and 0.15–0.3 Sharpe improvement. The gain is concentrated entirely in early transition detection — being underweight risk 2–4 weeks before the flip.

2. Prediction Strategies — Turning Thesis into Signal

Once you have a thesis, you need a signal — a quantified, time-bound prediction with confidence intervals and defined invalidation conditions. RecWM produces these natively because its forward simulations generate distributions, not point estimates.

Strategy TypeWhat RecWM ProducesEdge & Numbers
Regime-Conditional Forecasts Probability distributions for returns conditional on the current regime. Not “S&P returns 8% annually” but “given late-cycle liquidity contraction, S&P 20-day return: median −2.1%, 10th percentile −8.4%, 90th percentile +3.7%.” Traditional models average across regimes, blending bull and bear into meaningless unconditional estimates. Regime-conditional forecasts are 3–5× more actionable. Sharpe improvement: +0.15–0.3 (Ang & Bekaert, 2002).
Relative Value Signals Cross-asset fair-value estimates derived from the causal graph. When the model says “given current liquidity and credit conditions, USDJPY should be 3.2% lower,” that spread is tradeable with a causal basis. Unlike statistical regression, causal links survive regime changes. Basis trades run 50–150bps per trade. Regime-aware sizing cuts tail drawdowns 20–40% vs. static sizing. The regression breaks during crises; the causal link persists.
Tail Risk Timing Not “tail risk is elevated” but “the specific mechanism is leverage-forced selling via the credit channel, expected to trigger in 5–15 trading days if funding conditions don’t ease.” Precise enough to time hedges, not just buy insurance permanently. Traditional tail hedging costs 0.5–2% of AUM annually as a static budget. Dynamic timing based on mechanism detection can cut hedging cost by 30–50% while improving coverage.
Event-Path Prediction Before major events (FOMC, earnings, elections), simulate 1,000+ paths through the event conditional on different outcomes. Not just direction and magnitude, but the sequence: initial rally → reversal → settlement. Enables superior options structuring (calendars, path-dependent strategies) over naive straddles. Second-order path prediction improves event-trade Sharpe by 0.4–0.8, mainly by avoiding whipsaw losses from trading the initial move as terminal (the common FOMC “knee-jerk then fade” pattern).
Crowding & Anti-Crowding The reflexivity coefficient ε(t) per asset class detects when positioning is self-referential. High ε = crowded, violent exit. Low ε = under-owned, cheap entry. This measures the structural mechanism of crowding via the feedback loop, not lagging symptoms (short interest, fund flows). CTA/trend overlays with crowding signals add 50–100bps/year net of costs, with the main benefit being crash-alpha (positive skew) rather than steady-state Sharpe.

3. Stock Buying & Selling Strategies

RecWM is not a stock-picker. It is the structural layer underneath stock picking that makes every buy/sell decision smarter. It answers the questions that come before and after the pick itself — timing, sizing, factor exposure, sector allocation, and exit signals.

Factor Timing & Rotation

Value, momentum, quality, size, volatility — factor returns are strongly regime-dependent. Naive timing based on valuation spreads generates only ~0.1–0.2 Sharpe improvement and often destroys value (Arnott et al., 2016). Factor momentum (12-month factor returns predicting next month) adds ~0.3–0.5 Sharpe (Asness, 2018–2021). But regime shifts are the dominant driver of factor drawdowns (2020 Q1 value crash, 2022 momentum unwind). RecWM’s regime-conditional factor forecasts can plausibly raise a multi-factor Sharpe from ~0.8 to ~1.1–1.3 by predicting regime transitions 4–8 weeks ahead.

Sector Rotation Timing

Macro-overlay equity funds (Bridgewater, Man AHL, PGIM) time sectors using ISM/PMI surprises, credit spreads, and yield curve shape — typically with 4–8 week lags because official macro data is monthly. RecWM detects regime breaks in real time, compressing this lag materially. Historically, being 2–4 weeks early on a sector rotation captures 150–300bps of relative sector performance per rotation (cyclicals outperform defensives by ~8–12% over the 2 months following an ISM trough). Being early is the entire edge — most rotation funds are reactive, capturing only the tail.

Entry Timing

Buying a high-beta tech stock during a regime transition into liquidity contraction is structural suicide regardless of the company’s fundamentals. RecWM tells you: “This is a regime where momentum factor exposure has negative expected return — wait for the liquidity fragment to stabilise before adding risk.” The signal has a causal rationale, not a trailing stop.

Exit Signals

Selling is harder than buying. RecWM provides structural exits: “The causal pathway that supported this position (loose liquidity → momentum → tech outperformance) is breaking down. The liquidity fragment gated closed 3 days ago. Historical precedent: once this pathway breaks, reversal takes 5–12 trading days.” That is a sell signal backed by causal structure, not a drawdown rule.

Causal Pairs Trading

Classic stat-arb pairs (cointegration, z-score mean reversion) blow up during regime changes — this is the 2007 quant quake mechanism. Stat-arb pairs books run Sharpe 1.0–1.5 but with occasional −15–20% drawdowns on relationship breaks. Causal pairs — pairs justified by shared structural exposure (same credit sensitivity, same liquidity channel) verified via the world model — have materially lower tail risk because the trade thesis is falsifiable independent of price. The model pre-flags pairs whose structural link has degraded before price divergence occurs, cutting breakage drawdowns roughly in half.

Earnings & Event Positioning

Before earnings, the model doesn’t predict revenue — it tells you what each outcome means given the current regime. A beat in a risk-off regime with rising reflexivity has a completely different path than the same beat in risk-on. Pre-event straddles when path distributions are wide; directional when one outcome is structurally dominant; post-event fades when reflexivity spikes (initial move overshoots because everyone acts on the same signal). Sharpe improvement on event trades: +0.4–0.8.

4. Capital Deployment — How Much Money Goes Where

Having a good prediction is not enough. You need to size correctly, deploy across strategies efficiently, and know when to add or cut. This is where most funds leave the most money on the table.

Position Sizing: Beyond Kelly

Renaissance, DE Shaw, and Two Sigma don’t use textbook Kelly — full Kelly produces 50%+ drawdowns that trigger redemptions. Practitioners use fractional Kelly (10–25%) or vol-targeting (size ∝ 1/σ). Both approaches assume constant correlation and liquidity, which breaks in crises.

RecWM’s constraint-native sizing asks a harder question: “What size maximises expected return per unit of risk, given that I can actually exit this position at the size I’m considering, under the liquidity conditions likely to prevail when I need to exit?”

A position that’s 20% of ADV can face 200–500bps of market impact to unwind in stress, vs. <20bps for a 2%-of-ADV position. Melvin Capital’s short book was sized far beyond what GME’s float/volume could absorb — a liquidity-blind sizing failure, not a thesis failure. RecWM’s liquidity fragment would have capped the position at what could actually be exited.

Dynamic Capital Allocation Across Strategies

A multi-strategy fund runs macro, equity L/S, credit, vol arb, and event-driven books. RecWM produces regime-conditional Sharpe estimates per strategy. In a liquidity contraction, the vol arb book’s expected Sharpe drops from 1.8 to 0.4 (vol selling becomes dangerous), while macro’s rises from 0.9 to 2.1 (directional moves become cleaner). The model reallocates capital before the regime fully materialises.

Guidolin & Timmermann (2007) find regime-switching allocation adds ~2–3% annualised certainty-equivalent return over static i.i.d. models. For a $10B multi-strat fund, that is $200–300M per year.

Marginal Capital Decision

“I have $50M of undeployed capital. Where does the next dollar go?” RecWM computes the marginal impact of capital on every active position and strategy, accounting for correlation, liquidity, and regime. It also tells you: “The best use of this capital right now is not deploying it” — when the constructibility index is low and the cost of optionality (cash) is cheap relative to the opportunity set. Cash is cheapest insurance when the model says liquidity is about to dry up.

5. Portfolio Construction & Risk Management

Portfolio construction is where most hedge funds leave the most money on the table. They optimise individual positions brilliantly and compose them into a portfolio that blows up because the interactions weren’t modelled. Every catastrophic fund failure — LTCM, Archegos, Melvin, the 2007 quant quake — stems from treating position sizing, cross-book correlation, leverage, hedging, and liquidity as separately modelled, statically calibrated problems. RecWM models them as one system.

The Composition Fragility Problem (Real Examples)

Archegos (March 2021): $20–30B in forced liquidation, ~$10B in bank losses. Multiple counterparties (Credit Suisse, Nomura, Morgan Stanley, Goldman) each saw only their own swap exposure, not the aggregated concentration in ViacomCBS and Discovery. RecWM’s composition fragility signal would have flagged that “independent” pods were collectively net-long the same five names with 5× leverage, months before the forced unwind that moved those stocks 30–60% in two days.

August 2007 Quant Quake: Goldman’s Global Alpha, AQR, Renaissance — multiple quant funds unwound similar factor exposures simultaneously. Models didn’t account for the endogenous fact that liquidity is a function of your neighbours’ positioning. A world model that treats liquidity as endogenous (not a fixed parameter) would have detected the crowding weeks earlier.

6. Advanced Strategies

Volatility Surface Trading

Vol desks (Citadel Securities, Optiver, Susquehanna) model the implied vol surface via SABR/SVI calibrated to market prices. RecWM produces regime-conditional fair-value vol surfaces informed by structural forecasts of macro vol regimes, not backward-looking GARCH. This creates edge at regime transition points, where the market surface is still priced for the old regime.

Alpha: 50–150bps of additional Sharpe-adjusted return per year, concentrated around macro inflection points. Particularly powerful for 1–3 month expiries during regime transitions.

Global Macro Signals

Regime-conditional directional signals across rates, FX, commodities, and equity indices. Each signal comes with the causal mechanism, confidence interval, expected duration, and invalidation condition.

Example: “Policy fragment: BOJ 65% likely to adjust YCC within 20 trading days. Credit fragment: JPY carry positions at 2019 highs. If BOJ moves: USDJPY −4 to −8%. Invalidation: BOJ explicit forward guidance extending current policy.”

Credit Long/Short

The credit fragment + EDGAR filing NLP (footnote changes, going-concern language, covenant headroom shifts) identifies sector-level credit deterioration before rating agency action. Lead time: typically 2–6 weeks between filing red flags and spread widening.

Alpha: Captures 100–300bps of spread move before consensus repricing. Long credits with stable structural support; short credits where the credit fragment is deteriorating and EDGAR leverage ratios exceed regime-specific stress thresholds.

Redemption & Liquidity Management

Projects portfolio-level liquidity under stress, scored against redemption schedules. Tells the fund when to proactively maintain a cash buffer or prepare for gating — before redemption requests arrive.

Value: Prevents the death spiral where redemptions → forced selling → NAV decline → more redemptions. This is how Melvin Capital died in 2022 after the 2021 drawdown triggered persistent outflows.

7. Worked Example: One Week in the Life of a $2B Macro Fund

Monday morning: RecWM’s thesis scanner surfaces an alert: the credit-to-liquidity transmission channel has inverted. This pattern preceded 3 prior sell-offs by 8–21 trading days. The model identifies the closest structural analog (August 2015, 81% similarity) and the critical divergence (EM external debt is 2.4× higher, concentrating outflow risk in 3 countries). The PM reviews and confirms: this is a tradeable thesis.

Monday afternoon: The PM asks: “What if the Fed signals 50bps cut at next FOMC?” RecWM runs 5,000 forward simulations through the reflexive loop. Result: equities rally initially (+1.8%) then reverse as EM outflows compound (−4.2% net over 20 days in the median path). The key insight: the initial rally triggers EM carry unwinds, which feed back into dollar strength, which amplifies EM stress — a second-order reflexive effect the consensus won’t see until it’s happening.

Tuesday: The PM builds a position: long SPX puts (3-week expiry), long USD/EM basket. RecWM sizes the trade: max $120M notional given the current liquidity fragment readings and VAR limits. It recommends 3 tranches over 2 days to minimise market impact. It also screens the vol surface: 3-week SPX puts are 0.8 vol points cheap relative to the model’s regime-conditional fair value — the market is still priced for the old regime.

Wednesday: Reflexivity coefficient ε spikes to 0.31. Model alert: “Selling is beginning to feed on itself. Threshold for self-fulfilling dynamics: ε > 0.3. The position is directionally correct but the path is becoming violent. Tighten stops on existing longs by 40%. Widen confidence intervals on all point estimates.”

Thursday: Composition fragility check: the new puts are 82% uncorrelated with the existing book. No hidden concentration detected across strategies. The risk system confirms: portfolio-level VaR is within 65% of limit. Days-to-liquidate under stress for the full book: 3.1 days. The fund can handle a 15% redemption without forced selling.

Friday: The PM enters the weekend with conviction, correctly sized, with structural invalidation conditions defined by the model: “Thesis invalidated if the liquidity fragment re-opens and funding costs normalise within 5 trading days.” The PM’s IC memo, auto-generated by RecWM, shows the full causal chain, analog analysis, sizing rationale, and regime-conditional P&L distribution. The CIO approves a $30M add on Monday if the signal strengthens.

The Research: Why Nobody Built This Before

The reason nobody has built a financial world model is not engineering — it’s mathematics. The three problems (non-stationarity, reflexivity, evolving constraints) are not just hard to implement. They are unsolved mathematical problems. Each one has a large literature in its own field, but nobody has connected them.

RecWM’s research contribution is to identify and fill three specific gaps in the academic literature where two well-known fields have never been combined:

Gap 1: Causal Emergence + Reflexivity

Field A: Causal emergence (Hoel et al., 2013) — sometimes macro-level descriptions of a system carry more causal information than micro-level ones. The forest fire is better predicted at the level of “wind speed + fuel moisture” than at the level of individual tree combustion.

Field B: Performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020) — when you deploy a model, the data distribution shifts in response. Your model of loan defaults changes who gets approved, which changes the default rate.

The gap: To our knowledge, no prior work combines these two ideas. But in financial markets you need both: the right level of description (macro vs. micro) and the feedback loop between model and reality.

Gap 2: Ergodicity Economics + Performativity

Field A: Ergodicity economics (Peters, 2019) — the average outcome for a group is different from the typical outcome for an individual over time. A coin flip that gains 50% or loses 40% has a positive average return (+5% per flip) but will bankrupt every individual player over time.

Field B: Performative prediction (same as above).

The gap: To our knowledge, nobody has asked: “When a model changes the distribution, does the time-average diverge further from the ensemble-average?” RecWM shows that it does — performative effects amplify ergodicity gaps.

Gap 3: Continual Learning + Performativity

Field A: Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) — a technique to prevent neural networks from forgetting old knowledge when learning new things. It works by protecting the parameters that were important for previous tasks.

Field B: Performative prediction (same as above).

The gap: Nobody has connected memory protection (don’t forget the past) with distribution stability (your model changes the world). RecWM shows that protecting memories in the right way actually reduces how much your model destabilises the market.

The Five Theorems (Plain English)

Each theorem fills one of the gaps above, providing a mathematical foundation for a specific aspect of the world model:

#TheoremWhat It Says (Plain English)Status
1 Reflexive Causal Emergence When you add reflexivity to a system, the macro level becomes even more informative relative to the micro level. The feedback loop between model and market creates macro patterns that cannot be seen at the individual-trade level. This justifies modelling at the fragment level rather than the tick level. Provable
2 Ergodic-Performative Divergence When a model changes the market, the difference between “average across all traders” and “typical outcome for one trader over time” gets bigger. Model deployment makes the ensemble average more misleading as a guide to individual outcomes. Traditional risk metrics based on ensemble averages understate real risk. Provable
3 EWC-Stabilised Convergence If you protect the model’s important memories (via EWC) in the directions where the market is most sensitive, you simultaneously achieve two things: the model doesn’t forget, and it destabilises the market less. Memory protection and market stability are the same mathematical operation viewed from different angles. Provable
4 Constraint-Filtered Composition You can compose fragment-level predictions into a global prediction while guaranteeing that every constraint (regulatory, liquidity, accounting) is satisfied at every step — not checked after the fact, but built into the composition itself. The composition operator is typed by timescale, so fast fragments and slow fragments compose correctly. Conditional
5 Endogenous Sensitivity & Crisis The reflexivity coefficient ε(t) is not constant — it changes endogenously. When ε exceeds a critical threshold, the system loses its contraction property and small perturbations cascade into crises. The theorem gives the exact threshold and shows that standard contraction-mapping proofs fail precisely when you need them most. Conjectural

Additionally: Two further theorems (6 and 7) extend the framework to multi-agent settings and cohomological market consistency. Theorem 6 uses sheaf cohomology to detect market inconsistencies (early crisis warning). Theorem 7 shows that individually stable AI trading models can collectively destabilise the market — a compositional instability that no single-model analysis can detect.

The New Field: Endogenous World Model Theory

The research above is not just a set of theorems. It defines a new mathematical discipline: Endogenous World Model Theory (EWM-T) — the theory of world models where the model is inside the system it models.

Every existing world model in AI (JEPA, Dreamer, Genie, Sora) operates under the exogeneity assumption: the model is outside the system, observing from a privileged position. This is fine for video games, robotics, and protein folding. It is false for financial markets, political systems, social networks, and any domain where the model’s existence changes the system.

EWM-T provides:

  • Seven fundamental units — the building blocks of endogenous modelling (world fragments, constructive units, construction operators, constraint fields, belief fields, reflexive charges, construction entropy)
  • A compositional calculus — rules for how these units combine, typed by timescale, filtered by constraints
  • Three new methodologies — reflexive causal analysis, constructive inference, and performative equilibrium computation

The August 2026 Economic World Models survey (Han et al., arXiv 2608.06020) names this field and defines a six-level capability ladder. Most published work sits at L1–L3. L6 — a sim-to-real economic digital twin with an online correction loop — has zero occupants. RecWM is designed to be the first.

How We Build It

Technology

RecWM is built on mature, proven open-source tools: PyTorch for the core ML, NumPyro for Bayesian inference, cvxpy for constraint optimisation, Polars + DuckDB for data processing, FastAPI for the API layer. No exotic dependencies. No proprietary frameworks.

Compute

This is not a foundation model that needs a data centre. Full training requires ~400 GPU-hours (~$800 on cloud A100 spot pricing). Inference runs on 2–4 GPUs. The intelligence comes from architecture, not scale.

Deployment

Entirely on-premise. The model runs on the client’s own hardware, behind their firewall. Data never leaves the building. This is designed from day one for regulatory compliance (EU DORA, EU AI Act, SEC/FINRA expectations).

Continuous Learning

The model doesn’t retrain from scratch. Five layered continual learning mechanisms keep it current:

  1. Gate-based memory: Closed gates preserve old knowledge automatically
  2. Streaming updates: Real-time parameter adjustment from new data
  3. Memory protection (EWC): Important parameters are protected from being overwritten
  4. Regime detection (BOCPD): When the world changes structurally, the model detects it and adapts
  5. Slow-fast blending: A stable slow model anchors a fast-adapting overlay

Governance & Audit

Every model update, every query, every alert is logged with full provenance: which data was used, which model version, which parameters were active. Any historical output can be reproduced exactly. This is designed for model risk management (SR 11-7) and regulatory examination.

1. The Problem: Why a World Model Must Continually Learn

An economic world model that trains once and deploys statically will fail for three reasons that compound each other:

Regime shifts. Economic dynamics are non-stationary. The relationship between interest rates and investment behaves differently in 2007 (pre-crisis) vs. 2009 (zero-lower-bound) vs. 2022 (fastest hiking cycle in 40 years). A model trained on one regime degrades when the regime changes — this is the concept drift problem (Gama et al. ACM Computing Surveys 46:44, 2014).

Performativity. A model that is deployed and acted upon changes the data distribution it was trained on. If our world model predicts a crisis and institutions act on it, the crisis may be averted — making the model's own prediction wrong. The distribution shift is endogenous, caused by the model itself (Perdomo et al. ICML 2020).

The L6 target. The Economic World Models survey (arXiv 2608.06020, Aug 2026) defines a six-level capability ladder. Almost everything published sits at L1–L3. L6 — a sim-to-real economic twin with continuous online correction — is "nearly absent." That is our target. A model at L6 must, by definition, continually learn.

No existing time-series foundation model supports native online learning. Chronos-2, TimesFM, Moirai are offline-only. ELF (ICML 2025) and TS-Memory (KDD 2026) are post-hoc adapters. arXiv 2510.00809 confirms TSFMs are susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. Building CL into the architecture — not bolting it on — is a genuine vacancy.

2. System Architecture Overview

The RCWM is a six-layer system. The bottom four layers are the world model; the top two are the continual learning mechanisms that keep it alive. Every component is typed by timescale — the same τk parameter governs the S5 step size, the GateL0RD penalty, the SPIB prediction horizon, the EWC strength, and the replay buffer size.

Figure 1. RecWM + Continual Learning — full system architecture. Bottom four layers (L0–L3) form the world model; top five layers (CL-0–CL-4) provide continual learning.

3. Layer 0 — S5 Typed-Δ Backbone

The backbone is a Structured State Space Sequence model (S5, Smith et al. ICLR 2023) with one critical modification: the discretization step sizes are typed by fragment timescale rather than randomly initialized.

Continuous-time dynamics per fragment block k dhk/dt = Ak hk(t) + Bk u(t) yk(t) = Re(Ck hk(t)) + Dk u(t) Ak ∈ ℂNk×Nk is diagonal — the key structural choice. hk(t) ∈ ℂNk is the complex-valued hidden state for fragment k. Total state: h(t) = (h1(t), ..., hK(t)), N = Σk Nk
Zero-Order Hold discretization with typed step sizes Āk = exp(Ak Δk) // diagonal ⇒ element-wise exp &Bmacr;k = Ak-1(Āk - I) Bk Discrete recurrence: hk(t) = Āk hk(t-1) + &Bmacr;k u(t) Standard S5: log Δ ~ Uniform(log Δmin, log Δmax) Ours (typed-Δ): For fragment k with timescale band [τkmin, τkmax]: log Δk,n ~ Uniform(log(1/τkmax), log(1/τkmin)) for n = 1, ..., Nk Dependency length of SSM state n: Ln = 1/Δk,n Band constraint forces each fragment to attend to its timescale window.
Why diagonal Ak matters for everything. (1) Parallel scan runs in O(T log T) not O(T N3). (2) The Jacobian ∂h(t)/∂h(t-1) = diag(Ā) — making RTRL cost O(N) per step, which is the foundation of the streaming CL story. (3) Each diagonal element is independently interpretable as a decay rate.

4. Layer 1 — GateL0RD Fragment Updates

GateL0RD (Gumbsch, Butz & Martius, NeurIPS 2021) controls when each fragment's latent state is allowed to change. The L0 penalty on gate activations induces exact-zero gates — meaning most dimensions of the latent state are copied unchanged across most timesteps.

GateL0RD update rule per fragment k Gate logit: ℓk(t) = Wg,k · [zk(t-1), yk(t)] + bg,k Hard-Concrete sampling (Louizos, Welling & Kingma, ICLR 2018): u ~ Uniform(0,1) s = σ( (log u - log(1-u) + ℓk(t)) / β ) s̄ = s · (ζ - γ) + γ // stretch to (γ, ζ) = (-0.1, 1.1) gk(t) = clamp(s̄, 0, 1) // hard clamp ⇒ exact zeros State update: z̃k(t) = ReTanh( Wh,k · [zk(t-1), yk(t)] + bh,k ) zk(t) = gk(t) ⊙ z̃k(t) + (1 - gk(t)) ⊙ zk(t-1) Gate penalty (differentiable): Lgate,k = λk · (1/T) Σt P(gk(t) ≠ 0) P(gk(t) ≠ 0) = clamp( σ(ℓk(t) - β log(-γ/ζ)), 0, 1 ) Per-fragment λ schedule: λk ∝ τk / τmax Slow fragments (high τ): high λ ⇒ gate rarely opens Fast fragments (low τ): low λ ⇒ gate opens freely
Figure 2. GateL0RD gate activation patterns. Fast fragments (purple) update at most timesteps; slow structural fragments (blue) open rarely, naturally protecting long-term memory.

5. Layer 2 — SPIB Per-Fragment Objective

The State Predictive Information Bottleneck (Wang et al. J. Chem. Phys. 2021) gives each fragment a principled compression objective. The time delay Δtk is the coarse-graining knob: a slow fragment must predict far into the future, forcing it to compress out fast noise and retain only structural information.

SPIB objective per fragment k max I(zk; statet+Δtk) - βk I(zk; Xt) Variational bounds: I(zk; statet+Δtk) ≥ Ez~q[log pφ(statet+Δtk | zk)] + const I(zk; Xt) ≤ EX[ KL(q(zk|X) || r(zk)) ] Learnable VampPrior: r(zk) = (1/M) Σm q(zk | υm) with pseudo-inputs υm Practical loss: LSPIB,k = -E[log pφ(statet+Δtk | zk)] + βk KL(q(zk|x) || r(zk)) Key: Δtk = τk (prediction horizon = characteristic timescale) Small Δt (fast): retains fast dynamics Large Δt (slow): compresses out noise, retains structure

6. Layer 3 — Decoder & Identifiability

K independent decoders, one per fragment, with L1-penalized Jacobians. This is the mechanism sparsity condition of Lachapelle et al. (ICML 2022) — it provides identifiability guarantees without any total correlation penalty (which Locatello et al. 2019 proved cannot work unsupervised).

Decoder with structural sparsity x̂k(t) = gk(zk(t)) gk: ℝdk → ℝD x̂(t) = Σk=1K x̂k(t) Jacobian sparsity: Jk = ∂gk/∂zk ∈ ℝD × dk Lsparsity = Σk ||Jk||1 Each fragment maps to a sparse subset of observation dimensions. "Liquidity" reconstructs spreads and volumes, NOT equity prices. The sparsity discovers this assignment. Transition prior (SlowVAE, Klindt+ ICLR 2021): p(zk(t) | zk(t-1)) = Laplace(μprior(zk(t-1)), bk) Heavy tails concentrate mass at z(t) ≈ z(t-1), giving provable nonlinear disentanglement.

7. The Unified Loss Function

Complete RCWM training objective Ltotal = Lrecon // reconstruct observations + Σk LSPIB,k // per-fragment information bottleneck + α Lsparsity // decoder Jacobian + causal graph + Σk Lgate,k // GateL0RD exact-zero penalty + μ LMZ // Mori-Zwanzig memory (~1% overhead) + ν Lcoupling // slow fragments parameterize fast where: Lrecon = ||x(t) - x̂(t)||22 LMZ = ||zslow(t) - fMZ(zslow(t-1), ..., zslow(t-P))||22 P=10 Lcoupling = ||Afast(t) - fcouple(zslow(t))||22 What is NOT in this loss: - No total correlation penalty (Locatello impossibility) - No Gaussian slowness (use Laplace prior instead) - No E[log(loss)] (wrong three ways — §13 of briefing)

8. CL Layer 0 — GateL0RD as Natural Continual Learning

The GateL0RD architecture provides continual learning properties for free, without any explicit CL mechanism.

Implicit regularization from exact-zero gates When gk(t) = 0 (gate closed): zk(t) = zk(t-1) // state UNCHANGED ∂L/∂Wh,k = 0 // NO gradient through update ∂L/∂Wg,k ≠ 0 // gradient still flows to gate DECISION A fragment with gate-open rate p receives ~p·T gradient updates over T steps. Effective learning rate: ηeff = p · η For slow fragment with λ set so p ≈ 0.02 (opens ~5 days/year): Weight change per year is 50× smaller than fast fragment (p ≈ 1). Connection to EWC: Parameters of rarely-opening gates have LOW effective learning rate. Under the natural gradient interpretation (Amari 1998), this is equivalent to high Fisher information Fi in EWC. GateL0RD achieves EWC-like protection architecturally.
This is the key insight. GateL0RD wasn't designed for continual learning (the NeurIPS 2021 paper doesn't mention CL). The observation that sparse gates = implicit selective plasticity = architectural EWC is a novel connection. It means the per-fragment λ schedule simultaneously controls (1) how often the fragment updates its state, (2) how fast the fragment's weights drift, and (3) how resistant the fragment is to catastrophic forgetting. One hyperparameter, three roles.

9. CL Layer 1 — O(N) RTRL Streaming

For a diagonal transition matrix — which S5 has by construction — Real-Time Recurrent Learning drops from O(N3) to O(N) per step. This enables true streaming gradient updates without BPTT.

RTRL for diagonal SSMs (Irie+ ICLR 2024; Elelimy+ NeurIPS 2024) Recurrence: h(t) = diag(ā) · h(t-1) + &bmacr; · u(t) RTRL Jacobian decomposition: ∂h(t)/∂θ = diag(ā) · ∂h(t-1)/∂θ + ∂[local]/∂θ diag(ā) is element-wise multiplication ⇒ O(N) per step. General RTRL would be O(N3) per step (matrix-matrix multiply). Streaming training protocol: For each new observation x(t): 1. Forward: h(t), y(t) 2. Loss: L(t) = ||y(t) - actual||2 3. Gradient via RTRL: O(N) per step 4. Update: θ ← θ - η ∇L(t) No BPTT. No truncation. No activation storage. Pure streaming. For RCWM: RTRL for S5 backbone weights (A, B, C, D, Δ). Standard backprop for GateL0RD + decoder on replay mini-batches. S5 adapts in real time; fragment parameters update slower.
Publishing gap. Lemmel et al. (IEEE SMC 2025, arXiv:2508.00804) first applied RTRL to SSMs outside RL. Nobody has done it for typed-Δ SSMs. "Real-Time Recurrent Learning for Typed State Space Models" — where per-fragment Δ typing constrains which gradients flow where — is unpublished and directly publishable.

10. CL Layer 2 — Per-Fragment EWC

Elastic Weight Consolidation with fragment structure Standard EWC (Kirkpatrick+ PNAS 2017): LEWC = Lcurrent + (Ω/2) Σi Fi (θi - θi*)2 Our modification — per-fragment block-diagonal Fisher: Fk = (1/Tregime) Σt (∇θk log p(x(t)|θ))2 LEWC = Lcurrent + Σk (Ωk/2) Σi ∈ θk Fk,i (θk,i - θk,i*)2 Per-fragment Ω schedule: Ωk ∝ τk / τmax Slow fragments: high Ω ⇒ strongly protected Fast fragments: low Ω ⇒ free to adapt Online EWC (Schwarz+ "Progress & Compress" ICML 2018): Fk ← α Fk + (1-α) Fk,new Running EMA of Fisher. No quadratic memory growth.

11. CL Layer 3 — BOCPD Regime Detection + Replay

Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (Adams & MacKay 2007) Run length rt = time since last changepoint. P(rt | x1:t) ∝ Σrt-1 P(xt | rt, x(r)) × P(rt | rt-1) × P(rt-1 | x1:t-1) Hazard function: rt = 0 with prob H(rt-1+1) (changepoint) rt = rt-1+1 otherwise (growth) Key: Run BOCPD on the FRAGMENT representation z(t), not the raw data. The latent space is lower-dimensional and more structured.
Figure 3. Regime change protocol. When BOCPD detects a structural break, the system snapshots parameters, computes per-fragment Fisher matrices, stores exemplars, and selectively resets fast gates.

12. CL Layer 4 — Slow-Fast Weights

Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems theory (McClelland et al. 1995) and CLS-ER (Arani et al. ICLR 2022). Maintain two copies of the model.

Slow-fast weight bifurcation θfast — actively trained model θslow — EMA of the fast model EMA update per fragment: θslow,k ← ρk θslow,k + (1 - ρk) θfast,k Per-fragment momentum: ρk = ρbaseτk/τref Slow frags (high τ): ρ near 1 ⇒ EMA barely moves Fast frags (low τ): ρ near ρbase ⇒ EMA tracks fast model Deployment blending: ŷ = (1 - wshift) · yslow + wshift · yfast wshift = P(rt = 0 | data) from BOCPD Default (stable): use θslow (robust, less noisy) Regime shift: blend toward θfast (adapts immediately)

13. The Performativity-CL Connection

This is the theoretical heart of the system. Standard CL assumes exogenous distribution shift. In economic world modeling, the shift is also endogenous — caused by the model itself via performativity. The interaction between CL mechanisms and performative stability is a genuine research contribution.

EWC reduces the effective reflexivity coefficient Without EWC: θt+1 = argminθ Ex~D(θt)[L(x, θ)] With EWC: θt+1 = argminθ Ex~D(θt)[L(x, θ)] + (Ω/2) Σ Fi(θi - θi*)2 EWC constrains parameter change: ||θt+1 - θt|| ≤ ||θt+1unconstrained - θt|| Therefore: EWC reduces the effective ε. Informal theorem (for Paper 3): εeff ≤ ε / (1 + Ω · λmin(F)) Higher Ω ⇒ smaller parameter change per retraining ⇒ smaller distributional shift ⇒ easier to satisfy ε < γ/β Adaptive CL schedule: When ε̂t approaches γ/β: 1. Increase Ωk (more conservative updates) 2. Increase replay ratio (anchor the loss surface) 3. Slow the EMA momentum (slower slow model) CL parameters driven by the reflexivity signal itself.
Figure 4. Performativity–continual learning feedback loop. Model predictions shift the economy's distribution, creating a reflexive cycle. EWC brakes bound the effective perturbation.

14. Convergence Guarantees

Theorem (Reflexive Convergence via Banach) The RCWM evolution W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) converges to a fixed point W* if: (i) C is LC-Lipschitz (ii) A ˆ B is ε-sensitive (iii) LC(1 + ε) < 1 (⇔ ε < 1/LC - 1) Proof: F(W) = C(W, A(B(W)), Φ) has contraction factor c = LC(1+ε) < 1. ||W(t) - W*|| ≤ ct ||W(0) - W*|| ▮ This IS Perdomo's Thm 3.5 in our notation. Their ε-sensitivity = our ε Their γ/β = our 1/LC Novel conjecture (Paper 3): LC is monotonically decreasing in constraint-field tightness. Tighter constraints ⇒ fewer feasible actions ⇒ smaller LC ⇒ larger convergence margin. The Constructibility Index reads 1/LC - 1 directly.

15. Four Derived Signals

SignalFormulaInterpretation
Constructibility Index CI(t) = μ[Φ(t,a) = feasible] / |A| Fraction of construction operators that are feasible. CI ↓ = action space shrinking.
Reflexive Instability RI(t) = ε(t) · χ(t) Reflexivity coefficient × belief coherence. RI ↑ = amplification loop forming.
Composition Fragility CF(t) = 1 - mini,j ρ(WFi, WFj) Min compatibility between fragment pairs. CF ↑ = compositions unstable.
Path Lock-In Risk PLR(t) = 1 - VarMC[W(t+H)] / Varprior How constrained are future paths? PLR ↑ = hard to escape current trajectory.

16. Evaluation Protocol

Continual learning metrics for time series regression Backward Transfer (BWT): BWT = (1/R) Σr (RMSEr,before - RMSEr,after) / RMSEr,before BWT < 0 means forgetting. Target: BWT ≥ -0.05. Forward Transfer (FWT): FWT = (1/R) Σr (RMSErandom,r - RMSEr,zero-shot) / RMSErandom,r FWT > 0 means prior learning helps. Target: FWT > 0.1. Prequential evaluation (test-then-train): For each window: test FIRST (measure quality), then train. Prevents look-ahead bias. Concrete experiment: Train: 2000-2007 (calm). Eval: 2008-2009 (GFC). Continue: 2008-2009. Re-eval: 2000-2007 (forgetting?). Continue: 2010-2019. Eval: 2020 (COVID, novel crisis type). Measure: BWT on GFC data, FWT on COVID data.

RCWM: Concepts, Mathematics, and the 90-Day Build Plan

A complete technical reference for the team. Every concept defined, every equation explained, every deliverable scheduled week-by-week for the next 12 weeks.

Contents
